claim: The probability of the emergence of the rubber hand illusion increased with visual noise.
source: We found that: (1) the probability of the emergence of the rubber hand illusion increased with visual noise and was well predicted by a causal inference model involving the observer computing the probability of the visual and tactile signals coming from a common source
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental findings showing increased illusion probability with increased visual noise, supported by statistical analysis (F[2, 28]=22.35, p<0.001) and model predictions.

claim: The probability of the emergence of the rubber hand illusion was well predicted by a causal inference model involving the observer computing the probability of the visual and tactile signals coming from a common source.
source: We found that: (1) the probability of the emergence of the rubber hand illusion increased with visual noise and was well predicted by a causal inference model involving the observer computing the probability of the visual and tactile signals coming from a common source
evidence: The manuscript presents model fitting results showing that the BCI model fits the observed data well (Figure 2A) with specific parameter estimates.

claim: The causal inference model outperformed a non-Bayesian model involving the observer not taking into account sensory uncertainty.
source: (2) the causal inference model outperformed a non-Bayesian model involving the observer not taking into account sensory uncertainty
evidence: The manuscript reports model comparison results using AIC and BIC showing the BCI model provides a better fit than the FC model (Table 1).

claim: The prior probability of inferring a common cause for body ownership and visuotactile synchrony detection was correlated.
source: (3) by comparing body ownership and visuotactile synchrony detection, we found that the prior probability of inferring a common cause for the two types of multisensory percept was correlated but greater for ownership
evidence: The manuscript reports a significant correlation between psame values for the two tasks (Pearson correlation: p=0.002, cor = 0.71; Figure 3A).

claim: The prior probability of inferring a common cause was greater for ownership than for visuotactile synchrony detection.
source: (3) by comparing body ownership and visuotactile synchrony detection, we found that the prior probability of inferring a common cause for the two types of multisensory percept was correlated but greater for ownership
evidence: The manuscript reports that psame was significantly lower for the synchrony judgment task (0.65±0.04) than for the ownership judgment task (0.83±0.04, paired t-test: t=5.9141, df = 14, and p<0.001).

claim: Individual differences in rubber hand illusion can be explained at the computational level as differences in how priors are used in the multisensory integration process.
source: which suggests that individual differences in rubber hand illusion can be explained at the computational level as differences in how priors are used in the multisensory integration process
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between prior probabilities across tasks and the model's ability to capture individual differences through the psame parameter.

claim: The same statistical principles determine the perception of the bodily self and the external world.
source: These results imply that the same statistical principles determine the perception of the bodily self and the external world.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the finding that both body ownership and synchrony detection follow similar BCI principles with shared sensory parameters.

claim: Body ownership is automatic and perceptual in nature and depends on integrating sensory signals from multiple sensory modalities, including vision, touch, and proprioception.
source: This experience of the body as one's own, referred to as 'body ownership' (Ehrsson, 2012), is automatic and perceptual in nature and depends on integrating sensory signals from multiple sensory modalities, including vision, touch, and proprioception.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ehrsson, 2012, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Disturbances in bodily self-perception are observed in various neurological and psychiatric disorders.
source: Body ownership is also an important topic in medicine and psychiatry, as disturbances in bodily self-perception are observed in various neurological (Brugger and Lenggenhager, 2014; Jenkinson et al., 2018) and psychiatric disorders (Costantini et al., 2020; Keizer et al., 2014; Saetta et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies documenting these disturbances.

claim: Body ownership is a critical component of the embodiment of advanced prosthetic limbs.
source: and body ownership is a critical component of the embodiment of advanced prosthetic limbs (Collins et al., 2017; Makin et al., 2017; Niedernhuber et al., 2018; Petrini et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on prosthetic limb embodiment.

claim: In the rubber hand illusion paradigm, participants watch a life-sized rubber hand being stroked in the same way and at the same time as strokes are delivered to their real passive hand, which is hidden from view behind a screen.
source: In the rubber hand illusion paradigm, participants watch a life-sized rubber hand being stroked in the same way and at the same time as strokes are delivered to their real passive hand, which is hidden from view behind a screen.
evidence: This describes the standard rubber hand illusion procedure, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: After a period of repeated synchronized strokes, most participants start to feel the rubber hand as their own and sense the touches of the paintbrush on the rubber hand where they see the model hand being stroked.
source: After a period of repeated synchronized strokes, most participants start to feel the rubber hand as their own and sense the touches of the paintbrush on the rubber hand where they see the model hand being stroked.
evidence: This describes the typical phenomenology of the rubber hand illusion, which is established knowledge.

claim: The rubber hand illusion depends on the match between vision and somatosensation and is triggered when the observed strokes match the sensed strokes on the hidden real hand and when the two hands are placed sufficiently close and in similar positions.
source: The illusion depends on the match between vision and somatosensation and is triggered when the observed strokes match the sensed strokes on the hidden real hand and when the two hands are placed sufficiently close and in similar positions.
evidence: This describes established principles of the rubber hand illusion based on general knowledge in the field.

claim: Neuroimaging studies associate body ownership changes experienced under the rubber hand illusion with activations of multisensory brain regions.
source: Moreover, neuroimaging studies associate body ownership changes experienced under the rubber hand illusion with activations of multisensory brain regions (Ehrsson et al., 2004; Guterstam et al., 2019a; Limanowski and Blankenburg, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: Bayesian causal inference models have been used to explain the multisensory perception of external objects.
source: Among these types of models, Bayesian causal inference (BCI) models (Körding et al., 2007) have recently been used to explain the multisensory perception of external objects (Cao et al., 2019; Kayser and Shams, 2015; Rohe et al., 2019), including the integration of touch and vision (Badde et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using BCI models.

claim: In BCI models, the most likely causal structure of multiple sensory events is estimated based on spatiotemporal correspondence, sensory uncertainty, and prior perceptual experiences.
source: In BCI models, the most likely causal structure of multiple sensory events is estimated based on spatiotemporal correspondence, sensory uncertainty, and prior perceptual experiences; this inferred causal structure then determines to what extent sensory signals should be integrated with respect to their relative reliability.
evidence: This describes the general principles of BCI models, which is established knowledge in computational neuroscience.

claim: It has been proposed that the probabilistic model could be extended to the sense of body ownership and the multisensory perception of one's own body.
source: In recent years, it has been proposed that this probabilistic model could be extended to the sense of body ownership and the multisensory perception of one's own body (Fang et al., 2019; Kilteni et al., 2015; Samad et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical proposals.

claim: Samad et al., 2015 developed a BCI model for the rubber hand illusion based on the spatiotemporal characteristics of visual and somatosensory stimulation but did not quantitatively test this model.
source: Samad et al., 2015 developed a BCI model for the rubber hand illusion based on the spatiotemporal characteristics of visual and somatosensory stimulation but did not quantitatively test this model.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the methodology of a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: Fang et al., 2019 conducted quantitative model testing, but a limitation of their work is that they did not use body ownership perceptual data but an indirect behavioral proxy of the rubber hand illusion (reaching error).
source: Fang et al., 2019 conducted quantitative model testing, but a limitation of their work is that they did not use body ownership perceptual data but an indirect behavioral proxy of the rubber hand illusion (reaching error) that could reflect processes other than body ownership (arm localization for motor control).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of a previous study's methodology, supported by citation.

claim: The present study's first goal was to test whether body ownership is determined by a Bayesian inference of a common cause.
source: Thus, the present study's first goal was to test whether body ownership is determined by a Bayesian inference of a common cause.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's objective.

claim: A Bayesian observer would take into account trial-to-trial fluctuations in sensory uncertainty when making perceptual decisions, changing their decision criterion in a specific way as a function of the sensory noise level of the current trial.
source: Specifically, a Bayesian observer would take into account trial-to-trial fluctuations in sensory uncertainty when making perceptual decisions, changing their decision criterion in a specific way as a function of the sensory noise level of the current trial (Keshvari et al., 2012; Körding et al., 2007; Magnotti et al., 2013; Qamar et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes a key prediction of Bayesian models, supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Multisensory synchrony judgment is a widely used task to examine the integration versus segregation of signals from different sensory modalities.
source: Multisensory synchrony judgment is a widely used task to examine the integration versus segregation of signals from different sensory modalities (Colonius and Diederich, 2020), and such synchrony perception follows BCI principles (Adam and Noppeney, 2014; Magnotti et al., 2013; Noel et al., 2018; Noppeney and Lee, 2018; Shams et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on synchrony judgment tasks.

claim: Synchrony perception follows BCI principles.
source: Multisensory synchrony judgment is a widely used task to examine the integration versus segregation of signals from different sensory modalities (Colonius and Diederich, 2020), and such synchrony perception follows BCI principles (Adam and Noppeney, 2014; Magnotti et al., 2013; Noel et al., 2018; Noppeney and Lee, 2018; Shams et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating BCI principles in synchrony perception.

claim: 18 healthy participants naïve to the conditions of the study were recruited for this experiment (six males, aged 25.2±4 years, right-handed).
source: 18 healthy participants naïve to the conditions of the study were recruited for this experiment (six males, aged 25.2±4 years, right-handed; they were recruited from outside the department, never having taken part in a bodily illusion experiment before).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study's participants.

claim: All experiments were approved by the Swedish Ethics Review Authority (Ethics number 2018/471-31/2).
source: All experiments were approved by the Swedish Ethics Review Authority (Ethics number 2018/471-31/2).
evidence: This is a factual statement about ethical approval.

claim: Approximately 20–25% of healthy participants do not report a clear and reliable rubber hand illusion.
source: However, we know that approximately 20–25% of healthy participants do not report a clear and reliable rubber hand illusion (Kalckert and Ehrsson, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Three participants (two females) did not reach the inclusion threshold; therefore, 15 subjects participated in the main experiment (five males, aged 26.3±4 years).
source: Three participants (two females) did not reach this threshold; therefore, 15 subjects participated in the main experiment (five males, aged 26.3±4 years, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a factual statement about participant exclusion and final sample size.

claim: The rubber hand illusion was successfully induced in the synchronous condition; the participants reported perceiving the rubber hand as their own hand in 94 ± 2% (mean ± SEM) of the 12 trials when the visual and tactile stimulations were synchronous.
source: The rubber hand illusion was successfully induced in the synchronous condition; indeed, the participants reported perceiving the rubber hand as their own hand in 94 ± 2% (mean ± SEM) of the 12 trials when the visual and tactile stimulations were synchronous
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results.

claim: For every participant, increasing the asynchrony between the seen and felt taps decreased the prevalence of the illusion.
source: Moreover, for every participant, increasing the asynchrony between the seen and felt taps decreased the prevalence of the illusion.
evidence: This is a report of a consistent pattern observed across all participants in the experimental data.

claim: When the rubber hand was touched 500 ms before the real hand, the illusion was reported in only 20 ± 5% of the 12 trials.
source: When the rubber hand was touched 500 ms before the real hand, the illusion was reported in only 20 ± 5% of the 12 trials (noise level 0: 13 ± 4%, noise level 30: 21 ± 5%, and noise level 50: 26 ± 7%)
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results.

claim: When the rubber hand was touched 500 ms after the real hand, the illusion was reported in only 19 ± 6% of the 12 trials.
source: when the rubber hand was touched 500 ms after the real hand, the illusion was reported in only 19 ± 6% of the 12 trials (noise level 0: 10 ± 3%, noise level 30: 18 ± 5%, and noise level 50: 29 ± 6%; main effect of asynchrony: F[6, 84]=5.97, p<0.001
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results with statistical analysis.

claim: Regardless of asynchrony, the participants perceived the illusion more often when the level of visual noise increased.
source: Moreover, regardless of asynchrony, the participants perceived the illusion more often when the level of visual noise increased (F[2, 28]=22.35, p<0.001; Holmes' post hoc test: noise level 0 versus noise level 30: p=0.018, davg = 0.4; noise level 30 versus noise level 50: p=0.005, davg = 0.5; noise level 0 versus noise level 50: p<0.001, davg = 1; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results with statistical analysis.

claim: The BCI model fits the observed data well.
source: This BCI model fits the observed data well (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results and visual inspection of Figure 2A.

claim: Adding an additional parameter to account for observer-specific stimulation uncertainty in the BCI* model did not improve the fit of the BCI model.
source: First, we observed that adding an additional parameter to account for observer-specific stimulation uncertainty in the BCI* model did not improve the fit of the BCI model (Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison results shown in Table 1.

claim: The goodness of fit of the BCI model was found to be higher than that of the FC model.
source: Second, an important alternative to the Bayesian model is a model that ignores variations in sensory uncertainty when judging if the rubber hand is one's own, for example, because the observer incorrectly assumes that sensory noise does not change. This second alternative model based on a fixed decisional criterion is the FC model. The goodness of fit of the BCI model was found to be higher than that of the FC model (Figure 2, Table 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison results shown in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: The BCI model provides a better explanation for the ownership data than the simpler FC model that does not take into account the sensory uncertainty in the decision process.
source: This result shows that the BCI model provides a better explanation for the ownership data than the simpler FC model that does not take into account the sensory uncertainty in the decision process.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: The BCI model fits the combined dataset from both ownership and synchrony tasks well.
source: The BCI model fits the combined dataset from both ownership and synchrony tasks well (Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Individuals who displayed a higher prior probability of combining the basic tactile and visual signals and perceiving the visuotactile synchrony of the events also showed a greater likelihood of combining multisensory signals in the ownership task and experiencing the rubber hand illusion.
source: That is, individuals who displayed a higher prior probability of combining the basic tactile and visual signals and perceiving the visuotactile synchrony of the events also showed a greater likelihood of combining multisensory signals in the ownership task and experiencing the rubber hand illusion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation result between psame values for the two tasks.

claim: The body ownership task and synchrony task involved different processing of the visual and somatosensory signals for the participants, and this difference in behavioral responses was well captured when two different a priori probabilities for a common cause were used to model each task.
source: Thus, this analysis leads us to the same conclusion as that of the extension analysis. The body ownership task and synchrony task involved different processing of the visual and somatosensory signals for the participants, and this difference in behavioral responses was well captured when two different a priori probabilities for a common cause were used to model each task.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the transfer analysis results.

claim: Body ownership perception can be described as a causal inference process that takes into account sensory uncertainty when determining whether an object is a part of one's own body or not.
source: The main finding of the present study is that body ownership perception can be described as a causal inference process that takes into account sensory uncertainty when determining whether an object is a part of one's own body or not.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The probability of the emergence of the rubber hand illusion was better predicted by a Bayesian model that takes into account the trial-by-trial level of sensory uncertainty to calculate the probability of a common cause for vision and touch given their relative onset time than by a non-Bayesian (FC) model that does not take into account sensory uncertainty.
source: We found that the probability of the emergence of the rubber hand illusion was better predicted by a Bayesian model that takes into account the trial-by-trial level of sensory uncertainty to calculate the probability of a common cause for vision and touch given their relative onset time than by a non-Bayesian (FC) model that does not take into account sensory uncertainty.
evidence: This is a summary of the model comparison results.

claim: The prior probability of a common cause was found to be higher for ownership than for synchrony detection.
source: Specifically, the prior probability of a common cause was found to be higher for ownership than for synchrony detection, and the two prior probabilities were found to be correlated across individuals.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparison results between the two tasks.

claim: The two prior probabilities were found to be correlated across individuals.
source: Specifically, the prior probability of a common cause was found to be higher for ownership than for synchrony detection, and the two prior probabilities were found to be correlated across individuals.
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation analysis results.

claim: Body ownership is a multisensory perception of one's own body determined by an uncertainty-based probabilistic inference of a common cause.
source: We conclude that body ownership is a multisensory perception of one's own body determined by an uncertainty-based probabilistic inference of a common cause.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the results.

claim: This novel means to quantify the rubber hand illusion based on psychophysics is more appropriate for computational studies focused on body ownership than traditional measures such as questionnaires or changes in perceived hand position (proprioceptive drift).
source: This novel means to quantify the rubber hand illusion based on psychophysics is more appropriate for computational studies focused on body ownership than traditional measures such as questionnaires or changes in perceived hand position (proprioceptive drift).
evidence: This is an evaluative claim about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Previous attempts made to apply BCI to body ownership were conducted at the group level by the categorical comparison of experimental conditions.
source: Previous attempts made to apply BCI to body ownership were conducted at the group level by the categorical comparison of experimental conditions (Samad et al., 2015); however, such a group-level approach does not properly challenge the proposed models as required according to standards in the field of computational behavioral studies.
evidence: This is a factual statement about previous research methodology, supported by citation.

claim: Reaching errors tend to be relatively small, and it is unclear how well the reaching errors correlate with the subjective perception of the illusion.
source: The only previous study that used quantitative Bayesian model testing analyzed target-reaching error in a virtual reality version of the rubber hand illusion (Fang et al., 2019), but reaching errors tend to be relatively small, and it is unclear how well the reaching errors correlate with the subjective perception of the illusion (Heed et al., 2011; Kammers et al., 2009; Newport et al., 2010; Newport and Preston, 2011; Rossi Sebastiano et al., 2022; Zopf et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies examining the relationship between reaching errors and illusion perception.

claim: The present study contributes to our computational understanding of body ownership as the first direct fit of the BCI model to individual-level ownership sensations judged under the rubber hand illusion.
source: Thus, the present study contributes to our computational understanding of body ownership as the first direct fit of the BCI model to individual-level ownership sensations judged under the rubber hand illusion.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and contribution of the study.

claim: Computational approaches to body ownership can lead to a better understanding of the multisensory processing involved in this phenomenon than traditional descriptive approaches.
source: Computational approaches to body ownership can lead to a better understanding of the multisensory processing involved in this phenomenon than traditional descriptive approaches.
evidence: This is an evaluative claim about the advantages of computational approaches.

claim: The BCI framework informs us about how various sensory signals and prior information about body states are integrated at the computational level.
source: The BCI framework informs us about how various sensory signals and prior information about body states are integrated at the computational level.
evidence: This is a statement about what the BCI framework provides.

claim: Previous models of body ownership focus on temporal and spatial congruence rules and temporal and spatial 'windows of integration.'
source: Previous models of body ownership focus on temporal and spatial congruence rules and temporal and spatial 'windows of integration;' if visual and somatosensory signals occur within a particular time window (Shimada et al., 2009; Costantini et al., 2016) and within a certain spatial zone (Lloyd, 2007; Brozzoli et al., 2012), the signals will be combined, and the illusion will be elicited (Ehrsson, 2012; Tsakiris, 2010; Makin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a characterization of previous models, supported by citations.

claim: These models do not detail how this happens at the computational level or explain how the relative contribution of different sensory signals and top-down prior information dynamically changes due to changes in uncertainty.
source: However, these models do not detail how this happens at the computational level or explain how the relative contribution of different sensory signals and top-down prior information dynamically changes due to changes in uncertainty.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the limitations of previous models.

claim: Body ownership under the rubber hand illusion arises as a consequence of a probabilistic computational process that infers the rubber hand as the common cause of vision and somatosensation by dynamically taking into account all available sensory evidence given their relative reliability and prior information.
source: Instead of occurring due to a sequence of categorical comparisons as proposed by Tsakiris, 2010 or by a set of rigid temporal and spatial rules based on receptive field properties of multisensory neurons as implied by Ehrsson, 2012 or Makin et al., 2008, body ownership under the rubber hand illusion arises as a consequence of a probabilistic computational process that infers the rubber hand as the common cause of vision and somatosensation by dynamically taking into account all available sensory evidence given their relative reliability and prior information.
evidence: This is the proposed computational explanation based on the study's findings.

claim: The causal inference model has greater predictive power than classical descriptive models.
source: The causal inference model further has greater predictive power than classical descriptive models; in that, it makes quantitative predictions about how illusion perception will change across a wide range of temporal asynchronies and changes in sensory uncertainty.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the causal inference model.

claim: The 'time window of integration' model only provides temporal thresholds (asynchrony between two sensory inputs) above which multisensory signals will not be integrated.
source: For example, the 'time window of integration' model – which is often used to describe the temporal constraint of multisensory integration (Meredith et al., 1987; Stein and Meredith, 1993) – only provides temporal thresholds (asynchrony between two sensory inputs) above which multisensory signals will not be integrated (Colonius and Diederich, 2004).
evidence: This is a characterization of a previous model, supported by citations.

claim: The present causal inference model explains how information from such asynchronies is used together with prior information and estimates of uncertainty to infer that the rubber hand is one's own or not.
source: In contrast, the present causal inference model explains how information from such asynchronies is used together with prior information and estimates of uncertainty to infer that the rubber hand is one's own or not.
evidence: This is a claim about what the present model explains.

claim: Spatial congruence and other types of multisensory congruences would naturally fit within the same computational framework.
source: Even though the present study focuses on temporal visuotactile congruence, spatial congruence (Fang et al., 2019; Samad et al., 2015) and other types of multisensory congruences (e.g. Ehrsson et al., 2005; Tsakiris et al., 2010; Ide, 2013; Crucianelli and Ehrsson, 2022) would naturally fit within the same computational framework (Körding et al., 2007; Sato et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the generalizability of the framework, supported by citations.

claim: Our study supports the idea that individuals use probabilistic representations of their surroundings and their own body that take into account information about sensory uncertainty to infer the causal structure of sensory signals and optimally process them to create a clear perceptual distinction between the self and nonself.
source: Thus, in extending beyond descriptive models of body ownership, our study supports the idea that individuals use probabilistic representations of their surroundings and their own body that take into account information about sensory uncertainty to infer the causal structure of sensory signals and optimally process them to create a clear perceptual distinction between the self and nonself.
evidence: This is a broad theoretical conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Causal inference models of body ownership can be used in future neuroimaging and neurophysiological studies to investigate the underlying neural mechanisms of the computational processes.
source: From a broader cognitive neuroscience perspective, causal inference models of body ownership can be used in future neuroimaging and neurophysiological studies to investigate the underlying neural mechanisms of the computational processes.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research applications.

claim: One can test the hypothesis that activity in key multisensory areas closely follows the predictions of the BCI model and correlates with specific parameters of this model.
source: For example, instead of simply identifying frontal, parietal, and subcortical structures that show higher activity in the illusion condition compared to control conditions that violate temporal and spatial congruence rules (Ehrsson et al., 2004; Ehrsson et al., 2005; Guterstam et al., 2013; Limanowski and Blankenburg, 2016; Guterstam et al., 2019a; Rao and Kayser, 2017), one can test the hypothesis that activity in key multisensory areas closely follows the predictions of the BCI model and correlates with specific parameters of this model.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research possibilities.

claim: Neuronal populations in the posterior parietal cortex and premotor cortex could implement the computational processes of the uncertainty-based inference of a common cause of body ownership.
source: From previous neuroimaging work (Ehrsson et al., 2004; Guterstam et al., 2013; Limanowski and Blankenburg, 2016; Guterstam et al., 2019a), anatomical and physiological considerations based on nonhuman primate studies (Avillac et al., 2007; Graziano et al., 1997; Graziano et al., 2000; Fang et al., 2019), and a recent model-based fMRI study on body ownership judgments (Chancel et al., 2022), we theorize that neuronal populations in the posterior parietal cortex and premotor cortex could implement the computational processes of the uncertainty-based inference of a common cause of body ownership.
evidence: This is a theoretical speculation based on previous neuroimaging and neurophysiological evidence.

claim: The current study highlights the contribution of sensory uncertainty to body ownership by showing the superiority of a Bayesian model in predicting the emergence of the rubber hand illusion relative to a non-Bayesian model.
source: The current study highlights the contribution of sensory uncertainty to body ownership by showing the superiority of a Bayesian model in predicting the emergence of the rubber hand illusion relative to a non-Bayesian model.
evidence: This is a summary of one of the main findings.

claim: BCI is an often-used model to describe multisensory processing from the behavioral to cerebral levels.
source: Although BCI is an often-used model to describe multisensory processing from the behavioral to cerebral levels (Badde et al., 2020; Cao et al., 2019; Dokka et al., 2019; Kayser and Shams, 2015; Körding et al., 2007; Rohe et al., 2019; Rohe and Noppeney, 2015; Wozny et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a statement about the prevalence of BCI models, supported by citations.

claim: It is not uncommon to observe behaviors induced by sensory stimulation that diverge from strict Bayesian-optimal predictions.
source: it is not uncommon to observe behaviors induced by sensory stimulation that diverge from strict Bayesian-optimal predictions (Beck et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of Bayesian models, supported by citation.

claim: Some of these deviations from optimality can be explained by a contribution of sensory uncertainty to the perception that differs from that assumed under a Bayesian-optimal inference.
source: Some of these deviations from optimality can be explained by a contribution of sensory uncertainty to the perception that differs from that assumed under a Bayesian-optimal inference (Drugowitsch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about explanations for deviations from Bayesian optimality, supported by citation.

claim: Challenging the Bayesian-optimal assumption is a necessary good practice in computational studies.
source: Challenging the Bayesian-optimal assumption is thus a necessary good practice in computational studies (Jones and Love, 2011)
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation, supported by citation.

claim: Very few studies have investigated the role of sensory uncertainty in perceiving one's own limbs from a computational perspective.
source: However, very few studies have investigated the role of sensory uncertainty in perceiving one's own limbs from a computational perspective.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Studies explore the perception of limb movement trajectory, limb movement illusion, or perceived static limb position but not the sense of body ownership or similar aspects of the embodiment of an object.
source: Such studies explore the perception of limb movement trajectory (Reuschel et al., 2010), limb movement illusion (Chancel et al., 2016), or perceived static limb position (van Beers et al., 1999; van Beers et al., 2002) but not the sense of body ownership or similar aspects of the embodiment of an object.
evidence: This is a characterization of previous research, supported by citations.

claim: None of these previous studies investigate inferences about a common cause.
source: However, none of these previous studies investigate inferences about a common cause.
evidence: This is a statement about what previous studies did not investigate.

claim: A comparison between Bayesian and non-Bayesian models was also missing from the above-described studies of the rubber hand illusion and causal inference.
source: A comparison between Bayesian and non-Bayesian models was also missing from the above-described studies of the rubber hand illusion and causal inference (Fang et al., 2019; Samad et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about what previous studies did not do, supported by citations.

claim: The current results reveal how uncertainty influences the automatic perceptual decision to combine or segregate bodily related signals from different sensory modalities and that this inference process better follows Bayesian principles than non-Bayesian principles.
source: Thus, the current results reveal how uncertainty influences the automatic perceptual decision to combine or segregate bodily related signals from different sensory modalities and that this inference process better follows Bayesian principles than non-Bayesian principles.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: It is possible that people learn a criterion at each noise level, as one might predict in standard signal detection theory.
source: While we have argued that people take into account trial-to-trial uncertainty when making their body ownership and synchrony judgments, it is also possible that they learn a criterion at each noise level (Ma and Jazayeri, 2014), as one might predict in standard signal detection theory.
evidence: This is an alternative explanation considered by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: The authors believe it is unlikely that people learn a criterion at each noise level because they used multiple interleaved levels of noise while withholding any form of experimental feedback.
source: However, we believe this is unlikely because we used multiple interleaved levels of noise while withholding any form of experimental feedback.
evidence: This is a reasoning based on the experimental design.

claim: The results serve as the first conclusive empirical demonstration of BCI in a bodily illusion.
source: Thus, more broadly, our results advance our understanding of the multisensory processes that support the perception of one's own body, as they serve as the first conclusive empirical demonstration of BCI in a bodily illusion.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claim: Such successful modeling of the multisensory information processing in body ownership is relevant for future computational work into bodily illusions and bodily self-awareness.
